clue.text: Sat before fantastic Sunday lunch?

indicators.note: something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so the letters are reworked into a fanciful new order

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone sat down in good time for a marvellous Sunday lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sat before' reads as when you took your seat, but those nine letters are the raw material. The question mark flags that the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The roast joint of beef is the classic British Sunday family meal, so it is one example of such a dinner.

clue.text: Ply that's cut very fine

indicators.note: a word that has been cut is shortened, so it loses its final letter

parts.note: to ply someone with food and drink is to regale them

explanation.surface: Plywood sliced so thinly it is almost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ply' looks like the noun for a layer of wood, but it is the verb, to keep supplying someone with food or drink; dock the last letter of that synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Regal means fit for a king, magnificent and splendid, which is how something very fine looks.

clue.text: One that could — or couldn't? — bring to mind a riddle?

definitions.text: One that could — or couldn't? — bring to mind a riddle?

parts.words: One that could — or couldn't? — bring to mind a riddle?
parts.note: surface reading: something able, or perhaps unable, to call up a puzzling riddle
setter's reading: a riddle is also a coarse sieve, and a forgetful mind is compared to one

explanation.walkthrough: Riddle here is the old word for a garden sieve. A forgetful person's mind is said to be like one because everything falls through, hence it may or may not bring things to mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone forgetful whose recollections leak away like water through mesh, so their recall is unreliable.

clue.text: Shot played by Ashes batter, maybe, evaluating spin

definitions.text: Shot played by Ashes batter, maybe
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a drive (a straight attacking stroke) hit in a Test match, as an Ashes game is
second meaning: a trial run in a car before buying it

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator judges how well an England batter handles spin bowling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the England v Australia Test series in cricket, and a drive is a batting stroke. 'Spin' sounds like bowling but is a short ride in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A test-drive is a trial run in a vehicle to judge how it performs, so evaluating a car while taking a short ride.

clue.text: Quickly twisted sad news from journal's head office?

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the head of a journal's office
a death is sad news

explanation.surface: A newspaper's grim announcement from the top office, swiftly spun.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads as a headline: the editor died. That is the sad news from the head office.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that eddied swirled round in rapid circular currents, turning on itself fast.

clue.text: Energy provider, very good one, in food: ham, perhaps

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so the outer word wraps around

parts.note: fare is food served
a saint is a very good person, abbreviated ST
a ham is an overacting actor

explanation.surface: A list of things that give energy: something excellent, a food such as ham.
explanation.walkthrough: Ham looks like food on the list but is a hammy performer. ST for saint is the usual crossword 'good one'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast reactor is a type of nuclear reactor generating electrical power, so it supplies the grid.

clue.text: Defiant bachelor: nothing can stop what he is!

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap from within, so these letters plug the middle of another word

parts.note: a bachelor is unmarried
O looks like zero
B is the abbreviation for bachelor

explanation.surface: A stubborn single man boasts nothing will stop him staying single.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What he is' points back at the bachelor: he is unmarried.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unbowed has not bent the knee or submitted, remaining resistant and undaunted.

clue.text: New Year turned lively in square

indicators.note: lively things jump about, so the letters are jumbled into another order

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
Y is the abbreviation for year
taken as written

explanation.surface: Revellers turned out in their thousands to see in the New Year in a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like the place of the party, but it is the definition in its sense of old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: A square person is conventional and out of touch with fashion, the opposite of hip or cool.

clue.text: There's a case for butter, and one having more chocolate?

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
one having something is its owner

explanation.surface: An argument for butter, and for someone who likes extra chocolate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More chocolate' is a comparative of the colour, not a quantity of sweets: chocolate as a shade of brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocolate is a dark brown shade, so something more chocolate in colour is darker brown.

clue.text: Being left by Dutch with passport, maybe, one in red headpiece

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
a passport is one example of identification
someone in the red owes money, so is an ower
a hood covers the head

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the Dutch border with a passport and red hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' here is old Cockney slang for a wife (my old Dutch), not someone from the Netherlands; being left by her through death makes a man a widower.
explanation.definitionFit: Widowerhood is the condition of a man whose wife has died, so he has been bereft of his spouse.

clue.text: Old tyrant's sins you and I'd laid out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, joined by 'and'
the contraction without its apostrophe

explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'tyrant' is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Dionysius the Elder was the ruthless ruler of Syracuse in ancient Sicily, a byword for despotic cruelty.

clue.text: One next to do lively dance for a change

parts.note: in the sol-fa scale do is followed by re
a jig is a brisk folk dance

explanation.surface: A partner at a party joins in a lively dance for something different.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is not the verb but the first note of do-re-mi, and the note next to it is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A rejig is an informal word for a rearrangement or reorganisation, a modest alteration.

clue.text: Centre for trek, facility across lake, is free

indicators.note: the centre is the middle, so only the middle letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of the four
L is the abbreviation for lake
to do something with facility is to do it with ease

explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' sounds like a building at the centre, but it means effortlessness. It sits next to the lake letter rather than wrapping it.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a captive is to let them go, to liberate them from confinement.

clue.text: You must stop pilgrimage after upsetting ancient tribe

clue.text: Facts are put up on register — for polymath?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gen' is British slang for the facts or the lowdown. 'On' in a down clue puts the reversed word above the register.
explanation.definitionFit: A generalist has knowledge across many fields rather than one specialism, as a polymath does, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Fancied rogue's seductive embraces

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold within the arms, so the phrase holds the word inside it

parts.note: running across the two words

explanation.surface: A rakish charmer's seductive hugs were much desired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancied' looks like the reaction to the rogue's hugs, but it is the definition in its sense of supposed.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy that something is so is to suppose or imagine it, to conjecture without certainty.

clue.text: Start a fight

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to begin working in earnest
second meaning: a scrap or brawl

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an instruction to pick a fight; split it into two meanings of one hyphenated phrase, verb and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means begin vigorously, and the noun is a brief quarrel or bout of fisticuffs.

clue.text: Make portent involving youth predicting disaster

parts.note: to do is to make

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap something in, so one word surrounds another

a lad is a youth

explanation.walkthrough: DO for 'make' sits in front, then the omen wraps around the youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something doom-laden is heavy with foreboding, full of gloomy forecasts of catastrophe.

clue.text: Old PM was familiar with pop song

parts.note: David Lloyd George was British Prime Minister 1916 to 1922
to be familiar with someone is to know them
pop is what you call your own father

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister turns out to have known a pop song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like pop music but is Dad. The title is a well-known British rugby and army song sung to the tune of Onward, Christian Soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a comic British singalong, a ditty chanted on terraces and in barracks, so it is a song.

clue.text: Hamper: medium one, not large, is in fashion

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so letters are placed within another word
'not' says something is absent, so one letter is taken away

parts.note: style is fashion
L is the abbreviation for large

Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Clothes sizes: a medium, never a large, is what is fashionable in a basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' looks like a picnic basket noun, but it is the verb. The sizes M and L are swapped in effect: lose the large and put medium plus one in.
explanation.definitionFit: To stymie someone is to obstruct or thwart their progress, to impede and frustrate them.

clue.text: Group heading for Scotland Yard

indicators.note: the heading is what comes at the top, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard reads as one place but splits in two; 'Yard' is a courtyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A squad is a small team of people, such as police officers or players, working as a unit.

clue.text: Rambler getting stick before run

explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' is not an order instruction but a word in its own right: the old ERE.

clue.text: I note there's little room outside section of glacier

fa is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is a musical note from do-re-mi, not a remark.

clue.text: Hitch or take plane home, stopping at hotel on time — ten — surprisingly

parts.note: taken as written
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
taken as written
to fly in is to arrive home by air

clue.text: Inclined unfortunately to promote surfing primarily before books

clue.text: Bath for one to lie in really after one's dropped temperature

indicators.note: something dropped is let go, so a letter is left out

parts.note: a unit is a single one; the 's stands for has

where a thing sits is where it lies

clue.text: Stories being spread of a coup, ultimately baseless

parts.note: taken as written

parts.note: the final letter
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Baseless' looks like a judgement on the rumours, but its eight letters go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop's fables are the classic ancient Greek collection of short moral tales with animal characters.

clue.text: Old flame put out

parts.note: an old flame is a former partner
to put a question is to pose it

clue.text: Each to come up

parts.words: Clues roughened up for the solver

clue.text: When turning blue, tip of tongue was hanging out

parts.note: the opening letter

clue.text: High state of versatility — role-player's content!

explanation.definitionFit: An airdrop delivers supplies by parachute from aircraft, so aid literally descends from the sky to people in need.

clue.text: Worn out after month dealing with excavation

parts.note: DEC is the calendar abbreviation for December

a pit is a dug hole

explanation.definitionFit: Chromium plating on bumpers and trim is the gleaming metal finish that classic motors flaunt.

clue.text: Despot's wife moving a way back

parts.note: astir means up and moving about

clue.text: Targets relatives and friends

clue.text: Chapter in St John, maybe, one moving men to great effect

clue.text: Sacked a user, others being kept in one's place

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

clue.text: Trying hard to conceal aim with tweet

clue.text: Ruin suit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to finish someone off
second meaning: to be good enough for, to serve

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruin suit' looks like spoiling clothes; it is two verbs joined by nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to destroy someone and to be adequate or serve a purpose.

clue.text: Legal permission to broadcast ceremonies

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard over the air, so the word is identified by its sound

parts.note: legal permissions are entitlements under the law

explanation.surface: A licence to televise a solemn ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests broadcasting rights; 'to broadcast' is the cue to say the word aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Rites are formal religious or solemn acts performed in a set order, like a funeral or wedding.

clue.text: Missing uniform marred retinue fit for a queen

indicators.note: something marred is damaged and spoilt, so the letters are knocked out of order
something missing is absent, so a letter is removed

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Without matching costumes, a messy train of attendants looks fine for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit for a queen' is a stock phrase, but 'fit' is fodder and 'a queen' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefertiti was the Egyptian royal consort of Pharaoh Akhenaten, famed for her painted bust.

clue.text: Daily charge hitting the roof?

parts.note: the i is a British daily newspaper
a rate is a charge, as in a fee

explanation.surface: A daily fee that goes through the ceiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily charge' reads as a per-day fee, but the daily is the i, a British national newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To hit the roof is an idiom for flying into a rage, so someone doing it is furious.

clue.text: Change ending of popular film — oddly shocking treatment!

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable

indicators.note: oddly here means in the odd positions, so only the first and third letters are kept

parts.note: the first and third letters
ECT is electroconvulsive therapy, an electric shock treatment

explanation.surface: A hit movie's finale is rewritten, a strangely shocking way to treat it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change ending of popular film' reads as a director's cut, but only the first three words define, in the grammatical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatically, to inflect a word is to alter its form, typically its suffix, to show tense, number or case.

clue.text: Fancy putting answer forward without digressing

indicators.note: putting something elsewhere lifts it from its place, so a letter is removed before being set down again
moving forward means going to the front, so the lifted letter now leads

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
a dream is a fancy

explanation.surface: An imagined way to push one's reply forward without wandering off topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' says where the moved letter goes: the A in the dream moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad rem is Latin for to the matter, meaning relevant and keeping to the point at hand.

clue.text: Finally taking a very short vacation, acquiring fuel

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
something short is cut down, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the closing letter
taken as written
so means very, as in so good
hol is a British shortening of holiday, a vacation

explanation.surface: At last someone gets a brief break and fills up the tank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very short' reads as one phrase about a brief trip, but it splits: 'very' gives a word, and 'short' trims the holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasohol is motor fuel blending petrol with ethanol alcohol, used to power cars.

clue.text: Uncle Sam pauses to drop one off on time

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so a letter is left out

parts.note: to hesitate is to pause
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An American hesitates to drop someone off on time.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Sam looks like a person in the scene, but he personifies the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam is the national personification of the USA, standing for America as a whole.
